titleEn: The fool has said in his heart
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | Bb C | Dm Dm |
intro: Seven verses on a single accusation: not that anyone argues God out of existence, but that people behave as though nobody is watching. Almost the same poem appears again as Psalm 53, with a different divine name and a different verse 6, so reading the two side by side is the cleanest look you will get at how a psalm travelled and was re-edited. For a learner the useful pattern here is the negative existential particle ein, which shows up four times and carries the whole indictment: no God, none doing good, none, not even one.

stichs.en: A fool has said in his heart: there is no God.
They act corruptly, they make their dealings vile;
there is none who does good.

verses.summary: The premise and the consequence in one breath. The denial is spoken inwardly, never argued aloud, and what follows it is conduct rather than doctrine.

stichs.en: The LORD looked down from heaven on the children of man,
to see whether there is anyone with sense, anyone seeking God.

verses.summary: The camera reverses. Verse 1 was a man looking inward and finding nothing above him; here the looking runs the other way, and the search is for one person with sense.

stichs.en: Every one of them has turned aside, together they have gone rotten;
there is none who does good,

verses.summary: The answer to the search of verse 2, and it repeats the last line of verse 1 word for word before tightening it. The count goes from none to not one.

stichs.en: Do they not know, all these workers of iniquity,
who devour my people the way they eat bread,
and who have not called on the LORD?

verses.summary: The abstract corruption of verses 1 to 3 acquires victims. Eating is the image: my people are consumed as casually as a meal, without appetite or malice, which is the point.

stichs.en: There they were seized with dread,
for God is in the generation of the righteous.

verses.summary: The turn. Nothing is said to have happened to the wicked; what changes is that they are afraid, and the reason given is presence rather than punishment.

stichs.en: You would shame the counsel of the poor man,
but the LORD is his refuge.

verses.summary: The only verse addressed to the wicked directly, in the second person plural. Their target is not the poor man's body but his judgement, his plan, the thing they consider naive.

stichs.en: Who will give the deliverance of Israel out of Zion!
When the LORD turns back the fortunes of His people,
let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.

verses.summary: The psalm ends outside its own argument. Nothing in verses 1 to 6 has been resolved; instead the speaker asks for a rescue that has not arrived, and dates the joy to a future turning.

pardes.body: Three movements. Verses 1 to 3 state the charge and repeat it, verses 4 to 6 dramatise it with victims and a sudden fear, verse 7 breaks frame and asks for rescue. The keyword is the particle of non-existence: there is no God, there is none doing good, there is none, not even one. Notice that the fool of {{1.3}} never argues. He says it in his heart, and the psalm treats that as a practical position rather than a philosophical one, which is why the evidence offered against him is behaviour and not proof.

The word for fool at {{1.3}} is not a word for stupidity. It names moral collapse, and it is the name of the man in the Samuel narrative whose wife says that folly goes with him. The same root produces a verb meaning to wither and a noun for a carcass, so the fool is not the ignorant man but the one who has gone slack. In {{5.2}} the noun repeats its own verb, dread a dread, a cognate accusative that Hebrew uses to intensify: they were not merely afraid, they were afraid with fear. The opening of verse 7, {{7.0}} and {{7.1}}, is idiomatic: literally who will give, functionally if only.

This psalm appears twice in the book. Psalm 53 carries almost the same text with the divine name systematically changed and a different verse 6, which makes the pair the standard test case for how psalms were transmitted and reused in different collections. Readers have long taken the denial of verse 1 not as atheism but as a calculation: the fool grants that there is a God and bets that God does not look, which is why the psalm answers him in verse 2 with a God who does exactly that. The phrase turned back the fortunes in verse 7 was read in exile as a promise about return, and the psalm was said as a complaint that redemption had not yet come.

The mystical reading follows the withering sense of the root behind {{1.3}}: the fool is a soul that has fallen out of its own vitality, and his statement about God is a report on his own inner state rather than about heaven. On this reading verse 2 is not surveillance but attention seeking a channel, and the fear of {{5.2}} is what happens when a closed system is touched by a presence it had ruled out. The final verse then reads as the standard structure of redemption: the deliverance comes out of Zion, that is, from a fixed point that was there the whole time, and the two names Jacob and Israel mark the same person before and after the change.
